title: Philemon
hookLine: Paul sends a runaway slave back as a beloved brother; Christians later drew on this against slavery, too slowly

lines: PAUL SENDS HIM BACK, WITH A LETTER.
cards: It's a single short chapter, written to one household, and it's about one man. His name was Onesimus, and he was enslaved in the household of a Christian named Philemon.
At some point he left: whether he ran away or went looking for Paul's help, the letter doesn't say. He ended up with Paul, who was in prison, and there he became a Christian.
Now Paul is sending him back, with this letter in his hand.

teach.b: Paul could give orders, he says, but he'd rather ask. "I beseech thee for my son, whom I have begotten in my bands, Onesimus, Who hath been heretofore unprofitable to thee, but now is profitable both to me and thee."
The name Onesimus means useful, so readers hear a pun: once useless to you, now useful.

teach.h: NOT A SERVANT: A MOST DEAR BROTHER.
teach.b: Then the heart of the letter: receive him "not now as a servant, but instead of a servant, a most dear brother." A brother, in the flesh and in the Lord.
And Paul puts his own name on the line: if he owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write it with my own hand. I will repay it.

Now the hard part, said plainly. Paul never commands Philemon to set Onesimus free. He says he's confident Philemon will do even more than he asks, and readers have argued ever since about whether that's a hint.

teach.h: A LETTER USED ON BOTH SIDES.
teach.b: And this little letter was later used on both sides. Some slaveholders, including in the American South, cited it to defend returning people who had escaped.

teach.h: NOT NOW AS A SERVANT, BUT A MOST DEAR BROTHER.
teach.b: Others pointed to its words, no longer a servant but a brother, against slavery itself. Christians, the Catholic Church among them, came to condemn slavery too slowly.
Popes condemned the slave trade in the nineteenth century, and the Second Vatican Council listed slavery among the things that poison human society and insult the Creator.
Some years later, Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the church at Ephesus, named its bishop Onesimus. Some think it was the same man. Nobody can be sure.

how: The Catholic Church today condemns slavery as an offense against human dignity (Gaudium et Spes 27; Catechism 2414), and remembers Philemon and Onesimus in its readings and saints' calendars.

games.q: you're Paul. Onesimus has become a Christian in prison with you, and he belongs, by law, to Philemon. what do you do?
o: send him back with a letter: receive him as a most dear brother, and charge his debts to me.
send him back with no letter at all.
games.why: he sends him back with this letter: "not now as a servant, but instead of a servant, a most dear brother."

practice: Bring to mind the people you'd call brother or sister without thinking, then widen the circle to someone who serves you and whose name you don't know: a cleaner, a driver, a cashier, someone who picks the fruit you eat.
Picture them as clearly as you can, and let the word brother or sister sit next to them. If you pray, pray for them; if not, simply hold them in that word.

wordCard.voice: Philemon. Paul's short letter sending Onesimus back, not as a servant, but as a most dear brother. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek name meaning useful, profitable; Paul puns on it in Philemon 1:11.
